prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on the magic-wavelength trap and its realization as a reproducible neutral-atom clock with uncertainty at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part for optical lattice clocks, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The chair's first question is whether the magic-wavelength lattice is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. I think the evidence settles it. A comb is a ruler for optical frequency, and the Wineland-Haroche prize rewarded control of single quantum systems. Neither gives a way to interrogate a very large number of neutral atoms at once without the trap shifting the transition. The magic-wavelength condition does that, and it is what turns the statistical gain of many atoms into stability. The evidence is that several laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and others) now reach 1e-18 level systematics and agree in intercomparisons, that the same platform resolves gravitational redshift across millimetres, and that it has opened many-body clock physics. On the citation question, I would word it around the concept and its realization, and I would not name the redefinition of the second. The redefinition is supporting evidence of maturity but not a condition, and if it slips for years a prize that depended on it would look odd. Katori is the origin of the magic-wavelength lattice and the first strontium realization, and Ye took it to record accuracy and stability. That wording does not claim a single origin for the clock family, which answers Kroll's concern. I also accept the point that a prize is for what was discovered or invented, and the invention here is the lattice condition and not the precision it later allowed.
statement.case_against: The real risk is that a sceptical reader sees the lattice clock as the next step in a line already honoured twice, and that its discovery content is so far mostly bounds on constants and dark matter and not a new observed phenomenon. Kroll and Danielsson both press this, and I cannot fully dismiss it: IceCube delivered something nature had not told us before, and the clock has so far told us that nothing is drifting at a very small level. A second weakness is credit. Many groups built the cold-atom and ultranarrow-laser toolkit that made the clock work, and the two names cannot reflect that. I think a careful citation handles this better than adding a third name, since the limit of three people would then force a hard choice about whom to leave out.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers IceCube (B007) on the discovery-first principle, admits that B015 is the safer choice, and asks what nature told us that we did not know in the lattice-clock case.
responses.response: I respect the discovery-first principle and I do not think IceCube is in doubt scientifically. My answer to the question is narrower than he may want. Nature told us that a many-atom neutral lattice can be made to operate at the level where gravitational redshift is resolved over a millimetre and where the many-body interaction between atoms appears in the clock frequency. That is a new regime and not only a better number, though I grant it is less dramatic than a new messenger. I also note that he calls the Halzen-Karle-Spiering trio imperfect and the committee has not agreed on it, as Olsson would give only Halzen and Karle. I would not oppose B007 in a later year if the attribution is settled, but I do not think the unsettled names are a reason to give up a cleanly credited prize now. I would like to hear whether he would accept B015 if the citation is written around the lattice concept and its realization.

responses.point: Kroll supports B015 first but wants a citation that does not imply a single origin of the clock family, asks whether the redefinition of the second is a precondition, and raises a possible two-part prize with a measurement-driven discovery such as B007 or B057.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and have changed my draft citation to rest on the magic-wavelength lattice and its realization. On the redefinition I side with treating it as outside the citation. On a two-part configuration, I considered it seriously, but I come out against it. Each candidate that would be paired with B015 has an attribution problem: B007 has the Spiering and Olsson dispute, and B057 leaves out Chu and Borde and sits close to the 1997 prize. With a three-person limit, B015 takes two names, so a second part could hold only one person, and no candidate on the list can be honestly cut that way. I would sooner have one prize that is defensible than two parts of which one is weak. I withdraw nothing from my doubts about B057.

responses.point: Lindroth, as the atomic physicist, regards the other groups at PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN as confirmation of robustness and not as missing co-laureates, and argues that the magic-wavelength step is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree and I have kept that argument. In round 1 I asked her whether early lattice proposals by others affect Katori's priority. The chair's summary shows she has not yet answered, and I would still like to see it, because my own recollection is from memory and I am not an atomic-clock specialist. If the priority is secure, the two-name allocation holds. If not, I would want the citation wording to carry the weight and not the names. I also take her view that the many-body clock physics is a real extension of Ye's contribution, and I think it supports crediting Ye alongside Katori, but it is not essential to the core claim.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle graphene (B006) on the theory-then-experiment chain, but would not stand in the way of B015, and treats timing and maturity as his main reservation.
responses.response: His readiness to accept B015 matters to me. I keep my view that maturity and reproducibility across laboratories favour the clock now and B006 later, since the mechanism of the superconductivity is still unsettled and Yuan Cao and several other groups fall outside the three names. I would not call the delay a judgment on merit. I have moved B006 into my alternatives, in place of B024, partly for this reason and partly because B024 is the candidate on which I have a conflict. I would still like him to say what he would need to see in the B015 citation, and I think the wording around the lattice concept is a reasonable answer.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Ye's role is the original invention or a later, higher-performance realization of Katori's scheme.
responses.response: This is the right question for the citation. From my knowledge, Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first strontium realization, so the invention is his. Ye's contribution is the record accuracy and stability, the cavity-stabilized laser and systematic-evaluation work that made the clock a precision instrument, and the many-body strontium clock. I think the citation can say so by naming the invention and the realization to the record level, in that order, without ranking the two men. This is a judgment from my reading and I have not checked the primary chronology.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which the chair has marked as the main unresolved point.
Priority among early lattice-clock proposals and the weight of Ye's work against Katori's concept, which I recall from memory and have not verified.
Timing relative to the redefinition of the second: I treat it as outside the citation, but others may weigh it differently.
Whether Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig would accept B015 with the revised citation, and whether B007 attribution can be settled for a later year.
For my alternatives, how B055 handles the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit and the overlap with the 2016 prize, and how B006 handles Yuan Cao and the pairing mechanism.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits, so I have a subject and institutional connection to B024 (circuit QED) and would recuse on that candidate. I have dropped B024 from my alternatives for this round. My Chalmers ties to Eva Olsson, a colleague at the same university, are institutional only and not connected to any candidate in my preferred configuration. I have no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the other candidates I name, as far as my profile shows.
